plan.hypothesis: one-sample t-test: H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ = 0.2
assumptions: Known population standard deviation (or large sample approximation)
Single sample tested against a fixed null mean
One-sided test with alternative H1: μ > 0
scientific_notes: Effect size: Cohen's d = (μ1 - μ0) / σ = 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4
Power calculation uses the non-central t-distribution under the alternative
Rounding to smallest integer n ≥ continuous solution

answer.summary: For a one-sided one-sample t-test comparing a normally distributed outcome with a mean increase of 0.2 units (SD 0.5) against a null mean of 0, the minimum sample size to achieve 80% power at α = 0.05 is **41 participants**. This achieves an actual power of 80.86%, exceeding the 80% target. At the preceding sample size (n = 40), power is 79.97%, confirming that 41 is the minimum integer sample size meeting the power specification.
answer.method: One-sample t-test power calculation via the R package pwr (version 1.3-0), which inverts the noncentral t-distribution CDF. The effect size is Cohen's d = (μ₁ − μ₀) / σ = 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4. Calculation uses the exact noncentral t-distribution parameterized by degrees of freedom (n − 1), noncentrality λ = √n × d, and critical value from t(α, n−1). Sample size is determined by finding the smallest integer n such that power(n, d, α) ≥ 0.80.
assumptions: Outcome is normally distributed with mean μ and constant variance σ² = (0.5)²
Null hypothesis: μ = 0; alternative hypothesis: μ > 0 (one-sided, superiority)
Single sample of independent observations, each measured once
Test statistic t = (X̄ − 0) / (S / √n) follows t(n−1) under H₀
No multiple testing, no interim analyses, no multiplicity adjustment
limitations: Power calculation assumes the normal approximation is adequate; for small samples (n < 30) validity depends on underlying normality.
Effect size (d = 0.4) is assumed known and constant; sample size does not account for uncertainty in estimation of σ.
No attrition or dropout is modeled; achieved sample size must remain at n = 41 for claimed power.
One-sided test increases power relative to two-sided; direction of effect must be specified a priori.
Calculation does not address issues such as measurement error, confounding, or model misspecification beyond the specified t-test framework.

executions.code:
# One-sample t-test power and sample size calculation
# H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ = 0.2 (one-sided)
# Effect: mean increase 0.2 units, SD = 0.5
# Alpha = 0.05, target power = 0.8

library(pwr)

# Parameters
mean_diff <- 0.2    # Effect size in original units
sd <- 0.5           # Standard deviation
cohen_d <- mean_diff / sd  # Effect size (Cohen's d)
alpha <- 0.05       # Significance level (one-sided)
target_power <- 0.80  # Target power

cat("Study Design: One-Sample t-Test\n")
cat("H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ > 0 (one-sided)\n")
cat("Mean difference:", mean_diff, "units\n")
cat("Standard deviation:", sd, "units\n")
cat("Cohen's d:", cohen_d, "\n")
cat("Alpha (one-sided):", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size for target power = 0.80
# pwr.t.test uses d = effect size (Cohen's d), n = sample size per group (for one-sample, n is total)
n_continuous <- pwr.t.test(d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, power = target_power, 
                           type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$n

cat("Continuous solution (one-sided):", n_continuous, "participants\n")

# Round up to nearest integer
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat("Minimum integer sample size:", n_integer, "participants\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at the recommended sample size
power_at_n <- pwr.t.test(n = n_integer, d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, 
                         type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$power

cat("Achieved power at n =", n_integer, ":", power_at_n, "\n")

# Also check power at n-1 to confirm this is the minimum
if (n_integer > 1) {
  power_at_n_minus_1 <- pwr.t.test(n = n_integer - 1, d = cohen_d, sig.level = alpha, 
                                   type = "one.sample", alternative = "greater")$power
  cat("Power at n =", n_integer - 1, ":", power_at_n_minus_1, "\n")
  cat("\nConfirmation: n =", n_integer, "is the minimum integer achieving target power\n")
}

# Store result for reporting
result_n <- n_integer
result_power <- power_at_n
